title: Wes Anderson Picks Nine of His Favorite Criterion Films
description:
in Film |   	September 3rd, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

Many an inter­net cinephile has won­dered aloud if the Cri­te­ri­on Clos­et is a real pl
body:
in Film |   	September 3rd, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

Many an inter­net cinephile has won­dered aloud if the Cri­te­ri­on Clos­et is a real place, or just a set thrown togeth­er to make videos when famous direc­tors like Christo­pher Nolan, Fran­cis Ford Cop­po­la, or Jim Jar­musch drop by. It turns out indeed to exist, not only at Cri­te­ri­on’s offices in New York, but also else­where. The Cri­te­ri­on Mobile Clos­et, for exam­ple, has tak­en the label’s home-video library on the road since 2024, the 40th anniver­sary of the com­pa­ny’s foun­da­tion. If it comes to your town, queue up in as time­ly a fash­ion as pos­si­ble, and you may get the chance to enter and remain inside for three min­utes. That may sound brief, but no less an auteur than Wes Ander­son takes almost a minute less to make his cin­e­mat­ic selec­tions in the new video above.
The occa­sion was the Cri­te­ri­on Mobile Clos­et’s stop at the Hol­ly­wood Bowl, which coin­cid­ed with the three-night con­cert event Music from the Films of Wes Ander­son this past June. With a few days’ trav­el ahead of him, he picks out nine Cri­te­ri­on releas­es as view­ing mate­r­i­al to take along on “our road trip across Amer­i­ca.”
With an eye toward pleas­ing the entire fam­i­ly, he goes most­ly for “reli­able, stand­by” clas­sics, begin­ning with Alfred Hitch­cock­’s The 39 Steps and con­tin­u­ing on to Michael Pow­ell and Emer­ic Press­burg­er’s The Red Shoes (“my daugh­ter loves this movie”), and two from Ernst Lubitsch, Heav­en Can Wait and Design for Liv­ing — a pic­ture that must appeal to Ander­son on sev­er­al lev­els, not least in that it deals with Amer­i­cans in Paris, a set of which he’s long been a mem­ber.
Oth­er of Ander­son­’s more canon­i­cal picks include Pre­ston Sturges’ The Lady Eve with Bar­bara Stan­wyck, “one of the great­est actress­es in the his­to­ry of cin­e­ma, as every­body knows”; Stage­coach, which requires by way of intro­duc­tion only the name of John Ford; and, from Satya­jit Ray, not the cel­e­brat­ed Apu tril­o­gy (which Nolan took home) but Charu­la­ta, the inspi­ra­tion for the binoc­u­lar shots in his own Moon­rise King­dom. He also pulls from the shelf Syd­ney Pol­lack­’s Toot­sie (“remem­ber, Bill Mur­ray is in there”), a some­what more recent selec­tion. What stands out even more is the prac­ti­cal­ly brand new Flow, Lat­vian ani­ma­tor Gints Zil­balodis’ dia­logue-free adven­ture movie with only ani­mal char­ac­ters. It may have yet to pass the test of time, but if the man who direct­ed Isle of Dogs likes it — to say noth­ing of Cri­te­ri­on’s impri­matur — it’s sure­ly worth a watch.

Based in Seoul, Col­in Marshall writes and broad­casts on cities, lan­guage, and cul­ture. He’s the author of the newslet­ter Books on Cities as well as the books 한국 요약 금지 (No Sum­ma­riz­ing Korea) and Kore­an Newtro. Fol­low him on the social net­work for­mer­ly known as Twit­ter at @colinmarshall.

title: Why Inventing Color TV Was So Difficult
description:
in History, Media, Technology |   	September 4th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

Many who read this will remem­ber watch­ing tele­vi­sion on a blac
body:
in History, Media, Technology |   	September 4th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

Many who read this will remem­ber watch­ing tele­vi­sion on a black-and-white set at some point in their lives. Few­er will remem­ber doing so because only black-and-white sets exist­ed. Of course, your own expe­ri­ence will depend upon your coun­try of ori­gin. The Unit­ed States began the tran­si­tion to col­or tele­vi­sion in 1953, and more than half of its pop­u­la­tion owned col­or sets less than twen­ty years there­after. France’s sta­tions start­ed to change over in 1967, and the last one did so in 1983. South Korea, where I live, start­ed its own reg­u­lar col­or broad­casts in 1980, though at that point, those from the Amer­i­can Forces Net­work, Japan, and even North Korea could already be tuned in for years.
Today we all take col­or TV for grant­ed, but as the Pri­mal Space video above explains, its inven­tion was no sim­ple mat­ter. Still, it occurred much ear­li­er than most of us would imag­ine. In 1925, Scot­tish inven­tor John Logie Baird came up with the first tele­vi­sion, which involved pass­ing light through holes in a spin­ning disc onto a pho­to­elec­tric cell for trans­mis­sion through cables or radio waves. This sys­tem could only reg­is­ter the bright­ness of the light, pro­duc­ing a black-and-white image. But the mech­a­nism itself sug­gest­ed a means of intro­duc­ing col­or: enlarge the disc, add sep­a­rate sets of holes for red, green, and blue, and repro­duce a frame of each in quick, cycli­cal suc­ces­sion at the oth­er end, tak­ing advan­tage of the human eye­’s ten­den­cy to col­lapse them into a sin­gle image.
Baird first demon­strat­ed his col­or tele­vi­sion sys­tem in 1928. Though impres­sive, it also looked unlike­ly to per­form at a scale that could pro­duce a sharp, smooth mov­ing pic­ture. Oth­er engi­neers saw more tele­vi­su­al promise in the tech­nol­o­gy of the cath­ode ray tube, or CRT, which Japan­ese inven­tor Ken­jiro Takayana­gi had already har­nessed for his own black-and-white mechan­i­cal tele­vi­sion in the year before. The key com­po­nent was the icono­scope invent­ed by Vladimir Zworykin in 1933. “Essen­tial­ly the world’s first video cam­era,” it employed an inter­nal elec­tron gun to “scan” a cap­tured image into a trans­mis­si­ble elec­tri­cal sig­nal. Still, the ques­tion remained: how to do it in col­or?
Enter the Radio Cor­po­ra­tion of Amer­i­ca, whose abbre­vi­at­ed name more than a few of us will remem­ber from our child­hood TV sets. Hav­ing devel­oped a video cam­era “that took the incom­ing light and fil­tered it through spe­cial prisms to sep­a­rate the red, green, and blue,” con­vert­ing each into its own sig­nal, RCA then faced the prob­lem of deliv­er­ing the result to view­ers at home. None of the more than five mil­lion black-and-white sets already extant in the U.S. could receive those three sig­nals at all. The solu­tion involved using one elec­tron gun per col­or, each of whose sig­nals would be encod­ed so as to be hid­den in the exist­ing black-and-white tele­vi­sion sig­nal and then decod­ed by col­or sets. Con­sumers may not have tak­en up the tech­nol­o­gy all at once, but those who did in time for The Wiz­ard of Oz’s first broad­cast in 1956 sure­ly under­stood that col­or TV had a future.

title: Discover J.R.R. Tolkien’s Personal Book Cover Designs for The Lord of the Rings Trilogy
description:
in Art, Books, Design, Literature |   	September 3rd, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			
In some rare cas­es, adap­ta­tions and inter­pre­ta­tions of a lit
body:
in Art, Books, Design, Literature |   	September 3rd, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			
In some rare cas­es, adap­ta­tions and inter­pre­ta­tions of a lit­er­ary work can sur­pass the source. Despite hun­dreds of valiant efforts on the part of fans, film­mak­ers, game/toy design­ers, and radio pro­duc­ers, this has nev­er been true of the ful­ly-real­ized fan­ta­sy world in J.R.R. Tolkien’s The Hob­bit and The Lord of the Rings tril­o­gy (not that it’s ever been anyone’s intent). As we not­ed in a pre­vi­ous post, Tolkien’s fic­tion­al world is so intri­cate, its sources so vast and var­ied, that Corey Olsen, “The Tolkien Pro­fes­sor,” has made it his entire life’s work to open that world up to stu­dents and curi­ous read­ers, such as with his eight-part lec­ture series on The Hob­bit.

One might also add illus­tra­tors to the list of Tolkien inter­preters above who have—in the almost nine­ty years since The Hobbit’s pub­li­ca­tion and more than sev­en­ty years since the first appear­ance of The Lord of the Rings trilogy—done their best to visu­al­ize Tolkien’s world. But per­haps no one did so bet­ter than the mas­ter him­self. Long known as a visu­al artist as well as a lit­er­ary one, Tolkien left behind over 100 illus­tra­tions for The Hob­bit, one of which adorns 2011’s Harper­Collins 75th anniver­sary edi­tion of the book. He also cre­at­ed these orig­i­nal cov­er designs for each book in The Lord of the Rings tril­o­gy.


In the long and com­plex pub­li­ca­tion his­to­ry of Tolkien’s most famous of works, it’s unclear if these designs ever made it onto books pub­lished dur­ing his life­time, but the sig­il in the cen­ter of The Fel­low­ship of the Ring design (above), with its omi­nous eye of Sauron sur­round­ed by elvish runes and topped by the one ring, did grace the ele­gant, min­i­mal­ist cov­ers of the first edi­tion of the tril­o­gy. Tolkien’s art­work received a thor­ough treat­ment in a 1995 mono­graph J.R.R. Tolkien Artist & Illus­tra­tor, which cov­ers over 60 years of Tolkien’s life as an artist, and the mag­ic of flickr brings us this com­pendi­um of Tolkien illus­tra­tions.
Note: An ear­li­er ver­sion of this post appeared on our site in 2013.

title: 75,000 Patterned Paper Kites Cascade in Jacob Hashimoto's Largest-Ever Installation
description: Created from bamboo and printed Japanese paper, Jacob Hashimoto’s elaborate installations cascade from the ceiling to create a vibrant “cloud cano
body:
Created from bamboo and printed Japanese paper, Jacob Hashimoto’s elaborate installations cascade from the ceiling to create a vibrant “cloud canopy.” In his latest exhibition titled Giant Arc, ripples of color and pattern stretch from wall to wall as the nearly 75,000 kite-like elements cluster, repeat, and tease the floor. The monumental work, which just went on view at SFMOMA, marks the largest piece the artist has created to date.
As sun streams through the museum’s large windows and mixes with the light of the gallery, the feel of the installation changes throughout the day. Hashimoto conceives of the experience as a conduit to wonder for visitors of all ages, focusing on formal compositional elements like contrast, hue, and repetition to evoke the joy of the present. 

“The gravity of Giant Arc is its universality,” Hashimoto says in a statement. “This essential nature allows people to find what they might need in the work—mysteries if people want them, stories if people desire them, narratives to spin and twist, experimental maps and aerial geographies to explore.”
Giant Arc will be on view through mid-2028 in the museum’s ground floor gallery. Find more on the Hashimoto’s Instagram, and revisit our interview with the artist from 2022.


Photo courtesy of Jacob Hashimoto Studio

title: Go Behind the Scenes of Blackwing Pencils' Ode to Analog Creativity
description: Headquartered in Stockton, California, Blackwing is about finding the joy in analog creative tools at a time when digital devices consume our atte
body:
Headquartered in Stockton, California, Blackwing is about finding the joy in analog creative tools at a time when digital devices consume our attention. The manufacturer produces its signature pencils in a series of specialized factories in Japan, where the graphite cores are meticulously processed before being sent to a wood shop. In a behind-the-scenes video, the company shares how that process works, followed by how the utensils begin to take shape.
Sandwiched between slats of wood, individual pencils are then sliced and trimmed to their characteristic hexagonal shape. Yet another factory takes care of the painting and labeling, where depending on the style, the pencils can receive up to 10 coats of lacquer to achieve the final color and feel. And for the final step, the instruments journey to Stockton, where a proprietary machine attaches each eraser, and they’re inspected by hand before being boxed by the dozen.
Shop Blackwing in the Colossal Shop.

title: Denizens of a Crowded City Populate Erin Milez's Dense Paintings
description: Whether it’s scenes from the subway, streets, or Times Square, visions of New York City are often hectic and crowded. For Erin Milez, the hustle a
body:
Whether it’s scenes from the subway, streets, or Times Square, visions of New York City are often hectic and crowded. For Erin Milez, the hustle and bustle, but moreover the cramped spaces and tightness, characterize a new body of work going on view this month in Everything the Light Touches at Monya Rowe Gallery.
Milez recently moved from New York to Seattle, and she began to examine the nature of human connection, or the lack thereof, in urban spaces. Her expressive paintings draw on the visual language and subject matter of artists like George Tooker and Jacob Lawrence, who approached the theme of urban life through distinctive, figurative compositions. There’s also an unmistakable nod to the blocky, social realist style of Works Progress Administration (WPA) murals, which were often installed in civic spaces like post offices and libraries. For Milez, a similar dynamism informs her detailed, textural paintings, underscored by a very 21st-century sense of detachment.
“Walk Sign Is On”
There is a sense of closeness and intensity in Milez’s compositions that’s simultaneously meditative, as the artist renders light in golden hues and hints at symmetry. Characters are often squeezed into confined spaces or obscured by foliage and infrastructure, wedged together and yet almost completely self-concerned. A pair stopped beneath blossoming branches in “A Giving Tree,” for instance, find themselves in a situation that would be intimate were it not for their inwardness or reticency to say hello.
Other examples include a woman curled up on a crowded beach in “Pick Your Plot” and numerous passengers in “Subway” who are all individually tuned into their own electronic devices. Despite the crowded scenario, no one speaks to one another, and everyone appears calm. “I was surprised to find how many of the figures are cropped, particularly in their facial features,” Milez says of her own work. “This was my subconscious designing these people who are experiencing some sensory limitations, not using their full self to be attentive to the world.”
Everything the Light Touches runs from September 10 to October 24 in New York. See more on Milez’s Instagram.

title: 40 Filmmakers in 25 Countries Team Up for an Ode to Nature Shot Entirely on Super 8 Cameras
description: Before the iPhone essentially turned all of us into documentarians, the Super 8 camera offered a more democratic approach to filmmaking. Kodak int
body:
Before the iPhone essentially turned all of us into documentarians, the Super 8 camera offered a more democratic approach to filmmaking. Kodak introduced the analog format in 1965 with an eye toward amateurs and hobbyists interested in capturing the world around them, and today it remains a stalwart of the discipline, particularly for those drawn to the grainy, nostalgic qualities of shooting on film.
Ed Sayers, director and founder of the annual Super 8 competition and community called straight 8, tapped into the camera’s equalizing legacy for his latest project. Bringing together 40 collaborators in 25 countries across five continents, Super Nature is a collective ode to our planet. Rather than travel the world capturing the sights and sounds of far-flung locales, Sayers subverts the traditional documentarian approach by stitching together stories of people and creatures directly from their homes.



Participants include lauded photographers Gideon Mendel and Ami Vitale, who also founded Vital Impacts, alongside communities like the Enawene Nawe tribe in Brazil. Sayers invited several filmmakers from straight 8, and Greenpeace introduced his team to folks in the organization’s network, too. “I wanted them to feel very free. I made sure they were tuned into the spirit of what the film was trying to achieve, putting precious intimate moments and thoughts on a pedestal,” he tells Colossal. “Many had never used Super 8 before so we sent them cameras and taught them how to use them on video calls.”
Because the prompt had few guardrails, the difficulty came in making the final film appear cohesive and intentional. This meant finding where disparate segments fit together and which might offer an interesting and suitable segue to the next. “It was important that as an ensemble the stories came across as more than the sum of their parts,” Sayers says. “In the end, you’re watching one immersive story made and voiced by a chorus of people whom you meet and see in the film, captured on Super 8 just like all the animals and environments in the whole film.”
Alongside cinematic shots underwater, in air, and on land, Sayers also asked for glimpses of the filmmakers themselves, alongside narration that situates each frame into a larger portrait. He attributes the intimacy of Super Nature to this impulse as it showcases a sense of vulnerability and connection both in front of and behind the camera. Eleven languages and dozens of accents appear throughout, emphasizing the rootedness of each filmmaker.
In an age of AI and frictionless digital technologies, analog approaches to creation are ever more radical. Part of what continues to draw Sayers to film is that it requires more planning, intention, and an innate sense of when it’s time to act. “With Super 8 film, the roll only lasts a couple of minutes before it runs out, and there’s a cost to it. So suddenly you’re studying your subject and waiting for what you think it is a great moment, with the right light, before pulling the trigger,” he says. “Looking at your subject—be it a grasshopper or a glacier—with the eye or through an old camera with vintage glass is very different to whipping out your iPhone and taking 20 shots.”
Dice Rose carries a Super 8 camera through desert landscape with cacti and golden sunlight and flare, filmed on Super 8
This sentiment echoes the trailer’s opening line from one of the filmmakers, too: “It’s like it resets something in your brain. You feel part of things again.” 
Released by BFI Distribution, Super Nature is screening in the U.K. and Ireland this month, with several London showtimes. Find one in your area on the film’s website.
